p: ¿Qué significa «Now compare two sentences. When I arrived, she was cooking. She started cooking before I arrived, so when I arrived, the cooking was already in progress.»?
o: Ahora compara dos frases. Cuando llegué, ella cocinaba. Empezó a cocinar antes de que yo llegara, así que cuando llegué, la cocina ya estaba en curso.
Piensa en una historia. Hay un fondo, la situación, y hay los hechos, lo que ocurrió. El inglés usa dos tiempos distintos para estas dos partes.
Ahora: Cuando llegué, ella cocinó. Esto significa que empezó a cocinar después de que yo llegara. Es una secuencia: primero llegué, luego ella cocinó.
say: Now compare two sentences. When I arrived, she was cooking. She started cooking before I arrived, so when I arrived, the cooking was already in progress.

o: I'm so sorry! I was taking a shower, and then I was watching a film with the volume up. I didn't hear the phone.
The past simple tells the main events, one after another. I opened the door, I walked in, and I turned on the light.

p: ¿Cómo se dice «Cuarto, usa while para la acción larga, when para la corta, y recuerda que los verbos de estado no van en continuo.»?
o: Fourth, use while for the long action, when for the short one, and remember that stative verbs don't go in the continuous.
I thanked him a hundred times, and I invited him to a coffee. We were chatting for an hour, and now we are good friends.
There is also a second use. Two long actions happening at the same time. While I was cooking, my husband was setting the table.
say: Fourth, use while for the long action, when for the short one, and remember that stative verbs don't go in the continuous.

El pasado simple cuenta los hechos principales, uno tras otro. Abrí la puerta, entré y encendí la luz.
